The first thing that comes is the sound of rain on a tin roof I have never owned. It is a borrowed memory, perhaps from a book, or a film, or a grandmother’s story. I hear it anyway: a soft, insistent percussion, like a thousand tiny fingers drumming on a table, waiting for an answer. In that sound there is no urgency. The world can wait. The kettle can wait. The letter can remain unopened. Rain makes a permission slip for stillness. I think about how much of life is spent bracing for the next thing, the next email, the next bill, the next diagnosis, the next joy. Rain interrupts the schedule. It says: not yet. For a few minutes, you are allowed to be exactly where you are.

Then the rain stops, and the silence is so complete it feels like a held breath. In the silence, a memory arrives uninvited: a summer evening when I was nine, lying on my back in a field of cut grass, watching the sky turn from blue to violet to a bruise of stars. I remember the smell of hay and gasoline from a distant mower, the tickle of a blade against my ear, the sense that the earth was a huge, patient animal and I was riding on its back. I remember thinking, with a child’s terrifying clarity, that one day I would die. Not as a sad fact, but as a strange, electric truth. The stars did not care. The grass did not care. And somehow, that was comforting. The universe was indifferent, but it was also beautiful, and I was part of it, a temporary arrangement of atoms that could feel awe.

I think about temporary arrangements. A sandcastle. A friendship. A city skyline. A marriage. A sentence. Everything is a sentence, really, even the things that feel like paragraphs. We are all trying to say something before the period comes. Some of us shout. Some of us whisper. Some of us write long, winding clauses that never quite reach the point. I have been all of these. I have been a shout in a crowded room and a whisper in an empty one. I have been a comma, a pause, a semicolon, a question mark. I have been an ellipsis, trailing off into the dark.

There is a lighthouse on a cliff I visited once in winter. The wind was so cold it made my eyes water, and the sea was the color of gunmetal. The lighthouse was white and red, sturdy and stubborn, and it had been standing there for over a century. I climbed the spiral stairs, my breath loud in the narrow tower, and when I reached the top, I looked out at the water and felt small in the best way. The lighthouse didn’t care about my deadlines or my doubts. It just kept flashing: here I am, here I am, here I am. A warning and a welcome. I wondered how many sailors had seen that light and felt their chests loosen. How many had been saved by a single beam cutting through the fog. We all need lighthouses. Sometimes we are lighthouses. Sometimes we are ships. Sometimes we are the fog.

I have been the fog. I have been the thing that obscures. I have been the confusion that makes a person lose their bearings. I have also been the beam: a steady presence in someone else’s storm, even when I didn’t know I was shining. That is the strange thing about being alive. You never know which version of yourself someone else is seeing. You never know what small kindness will become a lighthouse for another person. A smile. A phone call. A bowl of soup. A sentence that says, I see you. I see you in the dark, and I am not going anywhere.

The afternoon has shifted. The light through the window is gold now, the color of honey and old paper. A fly buzzes against the glass, confused by the transparency. I understand the fly. I have spent hours bumping against invisible walls, certain that if I just try harder, I will get through. Sometimes I do. Sometimes the window opens. Sometimes I realize the window was never locked; I just had to push. And sometimes I realize I was never meant to go through that window at all. There was a door around the corner the whole time.

I think about doors. The ones we open. The ones we close. The ones we leave ajar, hoping someone will come back. The ones we slam. The ones we paint a different color and pretend we never walked through. I have a door in my mind that leads to a version of my life I did not choose. I visit it sometimes, but only briefly. It is a clean, well-lighted place, but it is not mine. My life is messier. There are dishes in the sink. There are unsent letters. There are books stacked on the floor because the shelves are full. There is a crack in the ceiling that looks like a river. There is a plant that is somehow still alive despite my neglect. There is a coffee mug that says “World’s Best Dad” that I bought at a thrift store even though I am not a dad. It makes me laugh. That is enough.

Enough. That is a word I am learning. Enough is not a failure. Enough is a boundary. Enough is a gift. I have enough. I have enough time to write this. I have enough breath to fill my lungs. I have enough memory to make a story. I have enough love, if I am brave enough to give it. The rain has started again, softer this time, a gentle tapping on the roof. It is not my roof, but for now, it is my sound. And I let it fill the room, and I let the words come, and I let the world be what it is: temporary, beautiful, and always, always arriving.
